title: Response to Steve Shaw (Massive Iron) - Going to WAR Over FRONT DELT training
summary: In a respectful response video to Steve Shaw (Massive Iron), NH argues that front delt isolation (front raises, especially cables) is not the cause of shoulder problems; high-frequency horizontal pressing is. He contends that a strong, even dominant, muscle protects its joint, that imbalance means undertrained antagonists rather than an overdeveloped muscle, and that raises offer a different, joint-friendly stimulus. He agrees front delts are the one muscle that needs isolation least and that rear and medial delts deserve priority, but says what should be dropped for bad shoulders is excessive horizontal pressing, not front raises.

claims.claim: He dislikes small channels name-dropping big ones for drama; he always asks permission before criticizing someone's opinion by name, though published programs and methods are fair game to critique without asking.
Steve Shaw advocates against front delt isolation, relying on horizontal and vertical presses instead.
Saying presses are all you need for front delts is true in that it gets the job done, not that it is optimal; for powerlifters it makes sense because they train the competition press.
Raises, front or lateral, give a different stimulus to the front delt than presses.

You can't condemn a lift because most people do it wrong; front raises are among the most butchered exercises (swinging, bending elbows, weird shoulder rotations), but there is a proper way to do them.
Lifters over 45 with bad shoulders have moved the most lifetime tonnage in horizontal and vertical presses, not front raises, so presses are the likely culprits.
Pete Rubish's bench issues were created by an overabundance of horizontal pressing; he even added curls to fix elbow problems from having too much triceps relative to biceps.
Powerlifting culture has shifted: five years ago suggesting curls on a powerlifting channel got you mocked; now channels like Elite FTS recommend curls for triceps issues.
From his experience, men who can no longer press due to shoulder injury can still do raises, especially with cables, and keep growing their shoulders, including viewers over 50.
If any muscle doesn't need isolation it is the front delt, probably number one; that is far more defensible than saying rows and chin-ups make biceps isolation unnecessary.
A muscular imbalance doesn't equal a dominant body part (the counterparts are just undertrained), and a dominant body part doesn't equal an imbalance if the other muscles are also developed.

Joint wear in later life is not natural; people in his home region work fields until 80-90 without bad knees, backs or shoulders. He blames the focus on horizontal presses for shoulder pain in 40s-50s lifters.
A very strong body part makes the joint it surrounds stronger than other joints; a weaker antagonist doesn't by itself cause injury.
Overdeveloped quads don't cause knee injuries; underdeveloped hamstrings and glutes do.
He wrecked his right knee playing football (soccer) and his left knee playing basketball; his knee problems went away once he built comically big quads along with posterior chain work.
He had many shoulder issues until he found ways to isolate the front delt without pressing stress on the AC joint and rotator cuff; his issues went away while still training rear and medial delts.
It is the training method (pressing), not the development of the muscle, that taxes the shoulder joint.
Nobody says don't train your lower back because it will hurt later; lower back isolation is actually recommended for safe squats and deadlifts. A stronger muscle is a safer muscle.
People who build lots of muscle when young keep it later in life, and as a natural it doesn't shrink unless you stop moving.
He agrees that rear and medial delts deserve priority for shoulder development; rear delts provide a shelf so the shoulder can stay tucked down while front delts press safely.
Weak rear delts let you lose bench form, round the shoulders and overuse the rotator cuff, leading to injury.
He doesn't care about being right, only about discussion; YouTube fitness is stagnant and needs ideas to keep moving.
Christian Thibaudeau's point that bodybuilders' front delts are 5x bigger than non-lifters' is sensationalism: the front delt is small, and bodybuilders' other muscles are also far bigger.
In enhanced pro bodybuilders the medial and rear delts are usually the biggest part of the shoulder, giving the round look; naturals' front delts tend to be in tune with the rest.
Comparing 'lifters' rear and medial delts to non-lifters moves the goalposts; bodybuilders train rear and medial delts heavily and would show similar 5x differences.
Veteran powerlifters have more shoulder problems than veteran bodybuilders because they must compete in the bench, which stresses the rotator cuff and AC joint; bodybuilders are free to use raises.
He had shoulder problems while powerlifting from benching too much, even while doing more rear delt work than now; now with more front delt isolation he has none.

When people injure their shoulders it's never the muscle but what's underneath; main culprits are internal rotation and presses. Internal rotation in front raises is possible but rare, while many bench with internal rotation.
Telling people to balance horizontal presses with overhead press often fails because most lack the mobility and form for OHP and only do partial reps, which can worsen imbalances.
He doesn't use full ROM on overhead press either, but you should at least lock the shoulders and hold the weight overhead to engage all the traps, which helps prevent shoulder injury.
A strong front delt prevents injury as long as rear and medial delts aren't completely lacking; strengthening a muscle prevents injury.
Sticking to only one type of movement for hypertrophy leads to overuse injury.
Powerlifters Dan Green (very heavy front raises, over 50 lbs) and James Strickland (side raises) use raises to build shoulder muscle without taxing the AC joint and rotator cuff.
Whether built by presses or raises, the front delt gets bigger and stronger; raises lack the pressing neural adaptation but add muscle that supports strength and injury resistance.
Kyphotic posture comes mainly from thoracic rounding and is carried into the bench; fix it by developing scapular muscles (traps, rear delts), not by dropping front delt isolation.
For shoulder pain, drop high-frequency horizontal pressing, especially without variation, not front delt work; a strong front delt prevents injury.

Shoulders feel better when people drop front delt work because they replaced painful presses with rear and medial delt work; adding cable front raises would have given more front delt gains without pain.

exercises.name: Front raises (cable or dumbbell)
cues: avoid weird shoulder rotation and internal rotation
exercises.why: different stimulus than presses, builds front delts without stressing AC joint and rotator cuff; usable when pressing hurts

exercises.name: Lateral raises
exercises.why: medial delt development, shoulder strength without pressing stress

exercises.name: Overhead press
cues: at least lock shoulders and hold weight overhead to engage traps
exercises.why: often done with poor mobility and partial ROM; not a reliable fix for horizontal press imbalance

exercises.name: Bench press
cues: tuck shoulders in and down on a rear-delt shelf
exercises.why: high-frequency horizontal pressing is the main culprit of shoulder pain

exercises.name: Rear delt work
exercises.why: provides shelf for shoulder stability on presses; priority for shoulder development

exercises.name: Curls
exercises.why: used even by powerlifters (Pete Rubish) to fix elbow issues from triceps/biceps imbalance
